# Sheaf-Style Gluing of Partial Sections with Missing Values

## Abstract

We give a fully formal, elementary development (in Lean 4 / Mathlib) of a model
of *partial sections* over an index set, together with the gluing and locality
theorems that make this model behave like the sections of a sheaf. The model is
deliberately minimal: a partial section is a function `ι → Option α`, recording
at each index `i` either a value `some a` or the absence of data `none`. This is
exactly the shape of a record (a row of a table, a configuration, a measurement
vector) in which some fields may be missing. We prove that compatible partial
sections glue uniquely, that a section is determined by its restrictions to any
cover, and that an arbitrary pairwise-compatible family admits a common
extension. These are the combinatorial core of the sheaf condition, specialised
to the simplest topology in which "openness" is tracked through the *support* of
the data.

All statements live in the namespace `PartialSection` in
`Catalog/Computation/SheafPartialSections.lean`.

## 1. Definitions

* **Partial section.** `PartialSection ι α := ι → Option α`. At index `i`, the
  value `f i` is `some a` (data present) or `none` (data missing).

* **Support.** `Support f := {i | f i ≠ none}` is the set of indices carrying
  data. It is the natural "domain of definition" of a partial section and plays
  the role of the open set on which a sheaf section is defined.

* **Compatibility.** `Compatible f g := ∀ i a b, f i = some a → g i = some b →
  a = b`. Two sections are compatible when, wherever both are present, they
  agree. They are allowed to be present on different indices; they must only
  never *contradict* each other.

* **Glue.** `glue f g i := Option.orElse (f i) (g i)`: take `f`'s value where it
  exists, and fall back to `g` otherwise. The glue is always defined (no
  hypothesis needed); compatibility only becomes relevant when we ask the glue
  to *faithfully* extend `g` as well as `f`.

* **Extension.** `h ⊒ f := ∀ i a, f i = some a → h i = some a`: `h` reproduces
  every value already recorded by `f`. `h` may additionally fill in indices
  where `f` was missing. This is the order-theoretic "information" relation:
  `h ⊒ f` means `h` is at least as informative as `f` and never overwrites it.

* **Restriction.** `restrict f U i := if i ∈ U then f i else none`: forget all
  data outside the set `U`. This is the sheaf restriction map along the
  inclusion `U ↪ ι`.

## 2. Basic structural lemmas

The membership lemmas `mem_support_iff`, `not_mem_support_iff` and
`exists_of_mem_support` translate between the predicate `f i ≠ none` and the
existence of a concrete value. Compatibility is reflexive (`compatible_refl`)
and symmetric (`compatible_symm`); it is *not* required to be transitive, which
is precisely why pairwise compatibility (Section 5) is the right hypothesis for
gluing families. The computation rules `glue_apply`, `glue_eq_left_of_some` and
`glue_eq_right_of_none` pin down the value of a glue case by case, and
`support_glue_eq_union` shows that gluing unions the domains:
`Support (glue f g) = Support f ∪ Support g`.

## 3. The binary gluing theorem

The heart of the development consists of four results.

* `glue_extends_left : glue f g ⊒ f`. The glue always extends its first
  argument, with no hypothesis: where `f` has a value, the glue keeps it.

* `glue_extends_right : Compatible f g → glue f g ⊒ g`. The glue extends its
  second argument *exactly when* the two sections are compatible. If `g` records
  `a` at `i` while `f` records a different `b`, the glue would return `b` and
  fail to extend `g`; compatibility rules this out.

* `glue_unique : h ⊒ f → h ⊒ g → Support h ⊆ Support f ∪ Support g → h =
  glue f g`. Any common extension that introduces no spurious data beyond the
  combined support *is* the glue. Thus the glue is the unique minimal common
  extension.

* `compatible_of_common_extension : h ⊒ f → h ⊒ g → Compatible f g`. If a common
  extension exists at all, the sections must have been compatible: `h` cannot
  simultaneously equal two different values at one index.

Together with `support_glue_eq_union`, these assemble into the central
equivalence

```
compatible_iff_exists_common_extension :
  Compatible f g ↔ ∃ h, h ⊒ f ∧ h ⊒ g ∧ Support h ⊆ Support f ∪ Support g.
```

This is the gluing axiom of a sheaf in its cleanest form: *local data can be
amalgamated into a global section if and only if it is pairwise consistent on
overlaps.* The forward direction constructs the glue; the backward direction
recovers compatibility from the mere existence of an amalgamation.

## 4. Locality (separation)

The second sheaf axiom — that a section is determined by its restrictions to a
cover — appears as

```
restrict_locality :
  (∀ i, ∃ j, i ∈ U j) → (∀ j, restrict f (U j) = restrict g (U j)) → f = g.
```

If the sets `U j` cover the index set and `f` and `g` agree after restriction to
every `U j`, then `f = g` everywhere. The proof is pointwise: each index `i`
lies in some `U j`, on which the restrictions coincide, forcing `f i = g i`.
This is the *separation* (or *monopresheaf*) condition; combined with Section 3
it makes `PartialSection` a genuine sheaf of data on the discrete index set.

## 5. Gluing arbitrary families

For an indexed family `s : β → PartialSection ι α` we define
`PairwiseCompatible s := ∀ b c, Compatible (s b) (s c)` and the amalgamation

```
familyGlue s i :=
  if some member of the family has a value at i then (a choice of such a value)
  else none.
```

`familyGlue` is `noncomputable`, using `Classical.choice` only to select, at
each index, one of the values offered by the family. The selection is harmless
precisely because of pairwise compatibility: all offered values coincide. We
prove

* `familyGlue_extends : PairwiseCompatible s → ∀ b, familyGlue s ⊒ s b`, and
* `glue_family_exists : PairwiseCompatible s → ∃ h, ∀ b, h ⊒ s b`.

Thus an arbitrarily large consistent collection of partial records can always be
merged into a single record that faithfully extends every member, generalising
the binary gluing theorem to families of any cardinality.

## 6. Why this formalizes sheaf-style data integration with missing values

In applications, a "global object" (a complete record, a full configuration, a
reconciled data set) is rarely observed directly. Instead one observes many
*partial* views, each missing some fields: different sensors report different
coordinates, different sources fill different columns, different surveys answer
different questions. The questions are then:

1. **Consistency.** When can these partial views possibly come from one global
   object? Answer: exactly when they are pairwise compatible — they never
   disagree on a shared field. This is `compatible_iff_exists_common_extension`
   and `PairwiseCompatible`.

2. **Integration.** Given consistency, how do we build the integrated record?
   Answer: glue them — `glue` for two, `familyGlue` for many — which is well
   defined and extends every input (`glue_extends_left/right`,
   `familyGlue_extends`).

3. **Uniqueness / no fabrication.** Does integration invent information? Answer:
   no — the glue is the unique common extension with support contained in the
   union of inputs (`glue_unique`), so it adds nothing that was not present in
   some source.

4. **Locality.** Is the integrated record pinned down by what we can see on
   each part of a cover? Answer: yes (`restrict_locality`), so the global
   reconstruction is unambiguous.

These are precisely the sheaf axioms — *gluing* and *separation* — read as a
theory of data integration. The use of `Option` to model missing values, rather
than partial functions or subtypes, keeps every construction first-order and
decidable in structure (only the family-level choice is noncomputable), making
the entire development elementary and machine-checked end to end.

Impact: This would provide a quantitative order parameter for emergent cognition in neural networks, connect deep learning to statistical physics and random matrix theory, and enable principled architecture/search methods that target reasoning-critical phases rather than brute-force scaling.
